title: Inequality kkt duality and optimality certificates

items.title: Inequality constrained programs, tangent cones, constraint qualifications, and KKT
items.statement:
Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$
be $C^2$. Let $p,m\in\mathbb N$ with zero allowed; when the target
dimension is positive, let $h:U\to\mathbb R^p$ and
$g=(g_1,\ldots,g_m):U\to\mathbb R^m$ be componentwise $C^2$, and when it
is zero use the unique empty map. The $C^2$ convention for positive
dimensions is [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]].
The smooth inequality program is to minimize $f(x)$ subject to
$h(x)=0$ and $g_i(x)\le0$ for every $i$. Its feasible set is
$C=\{x\in U:h(x)=0,\ g_i(x)\le0\ (1\le i\le m)\}$. A feasible point $x_*$ is
a local minimizer if some open neighborhood $V$ of $x_*$ satisfies
$f(x_*)\le f(y)$ for every $y\in C\cap V$.

At a feasible $x$, the active set is
$I(x)=\{i:g_i(x)=0\}$. The Bouligand tangent cone and linearized cone are,
respectively,
$$
T_C(x)=\{d:\exists\,t_k>0,\ t_k\downarrow0,\ d_k\to d,\ x+t_kd_k\in C\},
$$
and
$$
\mathcal L_C(x)=\{d:Dh(x)d=0,\ Dg_i(x)d\le0\text{ for every }i\in I(x)\}.
$$
Gradients are column vectors and $Dg_i(x)d=\nabla g_i(x)^Td$.

The linear independence constraint qualification (LICQ) holds at $x$ when the rows of $Dh(x)$ together with
$\{\nabla g_i(x)^T:i\in I(x)\}$ are linearly independent. MFCQ holds at $x$
when $Dh(x)$ has full row rank (its rows are linearly independent) and there is $w\in\ker Dh(x)$ with
$Dg_i(x)w<0$ for every active $i$; the latter condition is vacuous if
$I(x)=\varnothing$. Here full row rank for a matrix with zero rows is
understood vacuously.

The Mangasarian–Fromovitz constraint qualification (MFCQ) is the condition
just stated. The Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) system is the stationarity,
feasibility, dual-feasibility, and complementarity system below.

For $\nu\in\mathbb R^p$ and $\lambda\in\mathbb R^m$, the Lagrangian and KKT
system are
$$
L(x,\nu,\lambda)=f(x)+\nu^Th(x)+\lambda^Tg(x),
$$
$$
h(x)=0,\quad g(x)\le0,\quad \lambda\ge0,\quad \lambda_i g_i(x)=0\ (1\le i\le m),\quad \nabla_xL(x,\nu,\lambda)=0.
$$
The critical cone for a KKT tuple is
$\mathcal K(x,\nu,\lambda)=\mathcal L_C(x)\cap
\{d:\nabla f(x)^Td=0\}$. These definitions use the differentiability and
gradient conventions of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]],
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]].
items.strategy: Definition only; no phase proof is applicable.

items.title: Finite-dimensional convex program, Lagrangian dual, and Slater condition
items.statement:
A subset is convex when it contains the segment joining each pair of its
points ([[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]]). A function
$F:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ is proper if it never equals
$-\infty$ and is finite at at least one point. Its domain is
$\operatorname{dom}F=\{x:F(x)<+\infty\}$. Its epigraph is
$\operatorname{epi}F=\{(x,t):F(x)\le t\}$. It is closed convex when its
epigraph is a closed convex set. For a nonempty convex set $S$,
$\operatorname{aff}S$ is its smallest containing affine subspace and
$\operatorname{ri}S$ is its interior relative to $\operatorname{aff}S$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $m,p\in\mathbb N$ with zero allowed, let
$f_0,g_1,\ldots,g_m$ be proper closed convex functions on $\mathbb R^n$,
let $A\in\mathbb R^{p\times n}$ have full row rank, and let
$b\in\mathbb R^p$. Full row rank means that the rows are linearly
independent, vacuously when $p=0$. The common domain is
$D=\operatorname{dom}f_0\cap\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{dom}g_i$. The primal
problem is to minimize $f_0(x)$ over $x\in D$ satisfying $Ax=b$ and
$g_i(x)\le0$. An inequality is removable if, with
$D_{-i}=\operatorname{dom}f_0\cap\bigcap_{j\ne i}\operatorname{dom}g_j$,
$D_{-i}\subseteq\operatorname{dom}g_i$ and $g_i(x)\le0$ for every $x\in D_{-i}$.
Then $D=D_{-i}$, so removing that function and its inequality leaves the
feasible set unchanged. Remove such inequalities one at a time, recomputing
$D_{-i}$ after each deletion. An inequality that is nonpositive only on $D$
but whose function domain restricts $D$ is not removable. Unless stated
otherwise, the inequalities below are the remaining ones after only these
domain-preserving deletions. The primal value is
$$
p^*=\inf\{f_0(x):x\in D,\ Ax=b,\ g_i(x)\le0\text{ for all }i\}.
$$

For $\lambda\in\mathbb R^m_+$ and $\nu\in\mathbb R^p$, the extended
Lagrangian is
$$
L(x,\lambda,\nu)=\begin{cases}f_0(x)+\lambda^Tg(x)+\nu^T(Ax-b),&x\in D,\\+\infty,&x\notin D.\end{cases}
$$
The dual function and dual value are
$$
q(\lambda,\nu)=\inf_{x\in\mathbb R^n}L(x,\lambda,\nu),\qquad d^*=\sup_{\lambda\ge0,\ \nu\in\mathbb R^p}q(\lambda,\nu).
$$
The dual supremum is attained when some admissible $(\lambda,\nu)$ has
$q(\lambda,\nu)=d^*$; the optimal duality gap is $p^*-d^*$ when both values
are finite.

Slater's condition means that there is
$x_s\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f_0)\cap
\bigcap_i\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}g_i)$ with $Ax_s=b$ and
$g_i(x_s)<0$ for every remaining inequality. Relative interior is used in
the affine hull of each domain, so the domain need not have ambient interior.
items.strategy: Definition only; no phase proof is applicable.

items.title: A finitely generated cone in Euclidean space is closed
items.statement:
For any finite list $a_1,\ldots,a_m\in\mathbb R^n$, including the empty
list, the cone
$$
K=\left\{\sum_{j=1}^m t_j a_j:t_j\ge0\right\}
$$
is a closed convex subset of $\mathbb R^n$.
items.strategy:
1.1 Every $y\in K$ has a representation whose positive-coefficient vectors are linearly independent. Start with any nonnegative coefficient list and discard its zero coefficients. If its remaining vectors are dependent, take a nonzero relation $\sum_j c_j a_j=0$ and change its sign so some $c_j>0$. For the current positive coefficients $t_j$, put $s=\min_{c_j>0}t_j/c_j$. Replacing each $t_j$ by $t_j-sc_j$ preserves the represented vector, leaves every coefficient nonnegative, and makes at least one positive coefficient zero. Repeating at most $m$ times leaves an independent positive support. [given, choose, algebra]

1.2 Fix an independent index set $J$ and let $A_J$ have columns $a_j$, $j\in J$. Its Gram matrix $G_J=A_J^TA_J$ is invertible: for every nonzero $v$, $v^TG_Jv=\|A_Jv\|_2^2>0$ by independence. Put $B_J=G_J^{-1}A_J^T$, define $R_J(y)=B_Jy$ on $\mathbb R^n$, and set $L_J=(\sum_{r=1}^{|J|}\sum_{s=1}^n(B_J)_{rs}^2)^{1/2}$. Applying [F2] to each row gives $\|R_J(y)-R_J(y')\|_2^2\le L_J^2\|y-y'\|_2^2$, so $R_J$ is Lipschitz with finite constant $L_J$, hence continuous. On the closed subspace $S_J=\operatorname{span}\{a_j:j\in J\}$ it satisfies $A_JR_J(y)=y$. Hence $A_J(\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{|J|})= S_J\cap R_J^{-1}(\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{|J|})$ is closed: $S_J$ is closed by [F1], the nonnegative orthant is closed, and $R_J$ is continuous. For $J=\varnothing$ this cone is $\{0\}$, also closed. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 By step 1.1, $K$ is the union of the cones in step 1.2 over independent subsets $J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}$. There are only finitely many such subsets, so this union is closed. Each component is a convex cone, and directly taking nonnegative combinations shows $K$ is convex. [step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

items.title: A regular level set realizes every compatible second-order jet
items.statement:
Let $H:U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^q$ be $C^2$, let $x\in U$, and
suppose $DH(x)$ is surjective. If $d\in\ker DH(x)$ and
$$DH(x)z+D^2H(x)[d,d]=0,$$
then there is a $C^2$ curve $\gamma$ on the level $H=H(x)$ near $0$ with
$\gamma(0)=x$, $\gamma'(0)=d$, and $\gamma''(0)=z$. For $q=0$ the level is
all of $U$ and the statement is immediate.
items.strategy:
1.1 If $q=0$, then $H$ is the unique map into $\mathbb R^0$ and the level is all of $U$. The curve $\gamma(t)=x+td+\tfrac12t^2z$ has the required value and first two derivatives. [given, construct]

1.2 Now suppose $q>0$ and take the graph in [F1]. Put $v=D^2\psi(0)[d,d]$. Since $H(x+td+\psi(td))=H(x)$ for small $t$, [F2] and $\psi(td)=\tfrac12t^2v+o(t^2)$ give $DH(x)d=0$ and $DH(x)v+D^2H(x)[d,d]=0$. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 The compatibility equation for $z$ and step 1.2 imply $e=z-v\in\ker DH(x)$. Define $u(t)=td+\tfrac12t^2e$ and $\gamma(t)=x+u(t)+\psi(u(t))$. This curve stays on $H=H(x)$ by [F1]. Using [F2] and $D\psi(0)=0$ gives $\gamma(t)=x+td+\tfrac12t^2(e+v)+o(t^2) =x+td+\tfrac12t^2z+o(t^2)$, so its first two derivatives at $0$ are $d$ and $z$. [step 1.2, F1, F2, construct] ∎

items.title: Scaled KKT residual and convex normal cone
items.statement:
Use the program and dimensions of
[[def-inequality-constrained-program-and-kkt-geometry]]. For any $x\in U$,
$\nu\in\mathbb R^p$, and $\lambda\in\mathbb R^m$, define coordinatewise
$[v]_i^+=\max\{v_i,0\}$ and the scaled residual
$$
r_{\mathrm{KKT}}(x,\nu,\lambda)=\|\nabla f(x)+Dh(x)^T\nu+Dg(x)^T\lambda\|_2+\|h(x)\|_2+\|[g(x)]^+\|_2+\|[-\lambda]^+\|_2+\|\lambda\circ g(x)\|_2.
$$
The symbol $\circ$ denotes coordinatewise multiplication. The norm is the
Euclidean norm from [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and the norm of the
zero-dimensional vector is $0$.

For a convex set $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and $x\in C$, its (outward) normal
cone is
$$
N_C(x)=\{v\in\mathbb R^n:\langle v,y-x\rangle\le0\text{ for every }y\in C\}.
$$
This definition applies in particular when $C$ is closed and convex.
items.strategy: Definition only; no phase proof is applicable.

items.title: Farkas alternative for a finite linear system
items.statement:
Let $A\in\mathbb R^{r\times n}$ and $b\in\mathbb R^r$. Exactly one of the
following holds:

1. There is $x\in\mathbb R^n$ with $x\ge0$ and $Ax=b$.
2. There is $y\in\mathbb R^r$ with $A^Ty\ge0$ and $b^Ty<0$.

Inequalities between vectors are coordinatewise.
items.strategy:
1.1 Let $C=\{\sum_{j=1}^n x_j A_j:x_j\ge0\}$, where $A_j$ are the columns of $A$. This is a nonempty convex cone and is closed by [F1]. If $b\in C$, its nonnegative coefficients give alternative 1. If $b\notin C$, let $p$ be its nearest point in $C$ by [F2] and put $z=b-p\ne0$. [F1, F2, given, construct]

2.1 Applying [F3] with $c=0$ and $c=2p$ gives both $\langle z,p\rangle\ge0$ and $\langle z,p\rangle\le0$, hence $\langle z,p\rangle=0$. Applying [F3] to arbitrary $c\in C$ then gives $\langle z,c\rangle\le0$. In particular $A_j^Tz\le0$ for every column, and $\langle z,b\rangle=\langle z,p+z\rangle=\|z\|_2^2>0$. Thus $y=-z$ satisfies $A^Ty\ge0$ and $b^Ty=-\|z\|_2^2<0$, which is alternative 2. [F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The alternatives cannot both hold: if $Ax=b$ with $x\ge0$ and $A^Ty\ge0$, then $b^Ty=x^TA^Ty\ge0$, contradicting $b^Ty<0$. Step 1.1 produces one alternative in every case, so exactly one holds. [step 1.1, algebra] ∎

references.title: Boyd and Vandenberghe, Convex Optimization
references.locator: Chapter 5, Section 5.8, Farkas' lemma and the theorem of alternatives; the present proof uses Euclidean projection and proves the stated orientation directly.

references.title: Nocedal and Wright, Numerical Optimization, second edition
references.locator: Chapter 12, Section 12.3, printed pp. 339–341; projection onto a closed gradient cone yields the multiplier alternative.

items.title: MFCQ identifies the linearized and Bouligand tangent cones
items.statement:
For the $C^2$ program of
[[def-inequality-constrained-program-and-kkt-geometry]], if MFCQ holds at a
feasible point $x$, then
$$T_C(x)=\mathcal L_C(x).$$
items.strategy:
1.1 Take $d\in T_C(x)$ and use its defining feasible sequence $x+t_kd_k$, where $t_k\downarrow0$ and $d_k\to d$. For $h(x)=0$, Taylor expansion gives $0=h(x+t_kd_k)=t_kDh(x)d+o(t_k)$, hence $Dh(x)d=0$. For active $i$, feasibility gives $0\ge g_i(x+t_kd_k)=t_kDg_i(x)d+o(t_k)$, hence $Dg_i(x)d\le0$. Therefore $d\in\mathcal L_C(x)$. [given, F1, algebra]

1.2 Now take $d\in\mathcal L_C(x)$. Let $w$ be the MFCQ direction; if no inequality is active set $w=0$. Both $d$ and $w$ lie in $\ker Dh(x)$. When there are equality constraints, [F2] supplies a local graph $x+u+\psi(u)$ over this kernel; with no equalities use $\psi=0$. For $t>0$ small, define $u(t)=td+t^{3/2}w$ and $x(t)=x+u(t)+\psi(u(t))$. Then $h(x(t))=0$ and [F3] yields $x(t)-x=td+t^{3/2}w+O(t^2)$, so $(x(t)-x)/t\to d$. [given, F2, F3, construct]

2.1 If $i$ is active, Taylor expansion gives $g_i(x(t))=tDg_i(x)d+t^{3/2}Dg_i(x)w+O(t^2)+o(t^2)$. When $Dg_i(x)d<0$, its order-$t$ term makes this negative for all sufficiently small $t>0$. When $Dg_i(x)d=0$, MFCQ gives $Dg_i(x)w<0$, and its order-$t^{3/2}$ term dominates the remainder of order $t^2$. Inactive inequalities remain strict by continuity. Since there are finitely many inequalities, one positive $\tau$ works for all of them and every $0<t<\tau$. Thus $x(t)$ is feasible for such $t$. [step 1.2, given, algebra]

3.1 Taking $t_k=\tau/2^{k+1}$ gives feasible points with $t_k\downarrow0$ and $(x(t_k)-x)/t_k\to d$, so $d\in T_C(x)$. This proves $\mathcal L_C(x)\subseteq T_C(x)$; step 1.1 gives the reverse inclusion. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, construct] ∎

items.title: Critical directions are tangent to every positively weighted active inequality
items.statement:
Let $(x,\nu,\lambda)$ satisfy the KKT conditions for the program of
[[def-inequality-constrained-program-and-kkt-geometry]]. For every
$d\in\mathcal L_C(x)$,
$$
\nabla f(x)^Td=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad Dg_i(x)d=0\text{ for every }i\in I(x)\text{ with }\lambda_i>0.
$$
Thus the critical cone is the linearized cone with equality imposed on each
positively weighted active inequality.
items.strategy:
1.1 For $d\in\mathcal L_C(x)$, the equality term in stationarity vanishes, and inactive multipliers vanish by complementarity. Therefore $\nabla f(x)^Td=-\sum_{i\in I(x)}\lambda_iDg_i(x)d$. Every summand on the right is nonnegative because $\lambda_i\ge0$ and $Dg_i(x)d\le0$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 The sum in step 1.1 is zero exactly when each term with $\lambda_i>0$ is zero; because each such term is nonnegative, this is equivalent to $Dg_i(x)d=0$ for every positively weighted active index. That is the claimed equivalence and critical-cone description. [step 1.1, algebra] ∎

references.title: Nocedal and Wright, Numerical Optimization, second edition
references.locator: Chapter 12, Section 12.4, printed pp. 342–343, equations (12.52)–(12.54), the critical-cone characterization.

references.title: Boyd and Vandenberghe, Convex Optimization
references.locator: Chapter 5, Section 5.5, complementary slackness and KKT conditions.

items.title: Every Lagrangian dual feasible pair is a lower-bound certificate
items.statement:
For the convex program and Lagrangian dual of
[[def-convex-program-duality-and-slater-condition]], every primal feasible
$x$ and every dual feasible $(\lambda,\nu)$ satisfy
$$q(\lambda,\nu)\le f_0(x).$$
Consequently, when the primal feasible set is nonempty, $d^*\le p^*$.
items.strategy:
1.1 Since $x$ is feasible, $Ax-b=0$ and $g_i(x)\le0$. Since $\lambda_i\ge0$, this gives $L(x,\lambda,\nu)=f_0(x)+\sum_i\lambda_i g_i(x)\le f_0(x)$. The infimum defining $q$ is no larger than this particular Lagrangian value, so $q(\lambda,\nu)\le f_0(x)$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 The bound in step 1.1 holds for every primal feasible $x$ and every dual feasible pair. Taking the infimum over primal feasible $x$ and the supremum over dual feasible pairs gives $d^*\le p^*$ when the primal set is nonempty. [step 1.1, algebra] ∎

references.title: Boyd and Vandenberghe, Convex Optimization
references.locator: Chapter 5, Section 5.1, printed pp. 215–221; the Lagrangian dual function and weak-duality lower bound.

references.title: Zhiyuan Li, Convex Optimization, Lecture 5: Lagrange Multipliers and KKT
references.locator: Theorem 5.1 and complete proof in the weak-duality section.

items.title: A finite-dimensional convex value function has a support at relative-interior points
items.statement:
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional Euclidean space and let
$p:V\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be convex, never $-\infty$, and finite somewhere.
If $0\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}p)$ and $p(0)\in\mathbb R$, then
there is a linear functional $\ell:V\to\mathbb R$ such that
$$p(z)\ge p(0)+\ell(z)\qquad(z\in V).$$
items.strategy:
1.1 Let $W=\operatorname{aff}(\operatorname{dom}p)$. Since $0$ belongs to the domain, $W$ is a linear subspace; relative interior gives a ball about $0$ in $W$ contained in $\operatorname{dom}p$. If $W=\{0\}$, take $\ell=0$. Otherwise identify $W$ with a Euclidean coordinate space. The restriction of $p$ to that open ball is finite and convex, so [F1] makes it continuous at $0$. [given, F1]

2.1 In $W\times\mathbb R$, let $E=\{(z,t):p(z)\le t\}$ and let $\overline E$ be its closure. The set $E$ is convex, $(0,p(0))\in E$, and $\overline E$ is nonempty, closed and convex. Continuity from step 1.1 shows that $(0,p(0)-\epsilon)\notin\overline E$ for every $\epsilon>0$: choose $\delta>0$ so $p(z)>p(0)-\epsilon/3$ whenever $\|z\|<\delta$, while a sufficiently small open ball about $(0,p(0)-\epsilon)$ has $\|z\|<\delta$ and $t<p(0)-2\epsilon/3$, so it misses $E$. Thus $(0,p(0))$ is a boundary point of $\overline E$. [step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 For each positive integer $k$, project $z_k=(0,p(0)-1/k)$ onto $\overline E$, obtaining $y_k$. Since $(0,p(0))\in\overline E$, the projection distance is at most $1/k$, so $y_k\to(0,p(0))$. The unit vectors $a_k=(y_k-z_k)/\|y_k-z_k\|_2$ have a convergent subsequence by [F3], with unit limit $a=(s,\alpha)\in W\times\mathbb R$. For each $y\in\overline E$, [F2] gives $\langle a_k,y-y_k\rangle\ge0$; passing along that subsequence gives $\langle a,y-(0,p(0))\rangle\ge0$. [F2, F3, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 The epigraph contains every upward vertical ray, so the support inequality forces $\alpha\ge0$. If $\alpha=0$, points $(z,p(z))\in E$ for all sufficiently small $z$ and $-z$ in the ball from step 1.1 force both $\langle s,z\rangle\ge0$ and $\langle s,-z\rangle\ge0$. Hence $s=0$, contradicting $\|a\|_2=1$. Therefore $\alpha>0$. Setting $\ell(z)=-\langle s,z\rangle/\alpha$, the support inequality at $(z,p(z))$ yields $p(z)\ge p(0)+\ell(z)$ for $z$ in the domain; outside the domain the inequality is automatic because $p(z)=+\infty$. [step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

references.title: Boyd and Vandenberghe, Convex Optimization
references.locator: Chapter 5, Section 5.3.2, printed pp. 235–236; the Slater proof obtains a supporting affine lower bound to the perturbation value function.

references.title: Zhiyuan Li, Convex Optimization, Lecture 5: Lagrange Multipliers and KKT
references.locator: Theorem 5.3, full proof in the Slater and exactness section; it invokes a relative-interior subgradient theorem for the perturbation value function.

items.title: MFCQ gives KKT multipliers at a smooth local minimizer
items.statement:
For the $C^2$ problem of
[[def-inequality-constrained-program-and-kkt-geometry]], if $x_*$ is a local
minimizer and MFCQ holds at $x_*$, then there exist
$\nu\in\mathbb R^p$ and $\lambda\in\mathbb R^m_+$ such that
$(x_*,\nu,\lambda)$ satisfies the KKT system.
items.strategy:
1.1 Every $d\in T_C(x_*)$ satisfies $
abla f(x_*)^Td\ge0$. For $d=0$ this is immediate. Otherwise take a defining sequence $x_*+t_kd_k\in C$, with $t_k\downarrow0$ and $d_k	o d$. For large $k$, local minimality gives $f(x_*+t_kd_k)-f(x_*)\ge0$. Differentiability gives $f(x_*+t_kd_k)-f(x_*)=t_k
abla f(x_*)^Td_k+o(t_k)$; divide by $t_k$ and pass to the limit. [given, algebra]

2.1 By [F1] and step 1.1, $
abla f(x_*)^Td\ge0$ for every $d\in\mathcal L_C(x_*)$. Form a matrix $B$ with columns $
abla h_j(x_*),-
abla h_j(x_*)$ for each equality and $-
abla g_i(x_*)$ for each active inequality, and set $c=
abla f(x_*)$. If alternative 1 of [F2] failed, alternative 2 would give $B^Td\ge0$ and $c^Td<0$. The paired equality columns force $Dh(x_*)d=0$, while the inequality columns force $Dg_i(x_*)d\le0$ for every active $i$, so $d\in\mathcal L_C(x_*)$, contradicting step 1.1. Thus there are nonnegative coefficients representing $c$ as a combination of the columns of $B$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Write the equality-column coefficients as $\alpha_j, eta_j\ge0$ and the active inequality coefficients as $\lambda_i\ge0$. The representation from step 2.1 is $
abla f(x_*)=Dh(x_*)^T(\alpha- eta)-Dg_{I(x_*)}(x_*)^T\lambda_I$. Set $
u=-(\alpha- eta)$ and set $\lambda_i=0$ for inactive $i$. Then stationarity holds. Feasibility holds because $x_*\in C$; dual feasibility holds by construction; and complementarity holds because active constraints vanish while inactive multipliers are zero. These are exactly the KKT conditions. [step 2.1, given, algebra] ∎

references.title: Nocedal and Wright, Numerical Optimization, second edition
references.locator: Chapter 12, Sections 12.2–12.5, printed pp. 327–353; KKT under LICQ and the statement that MFCQ also supplies first-order multipliers. The inequality sign convention is translated.

references.title: Boyd and Vandenberghe, Convex Optimization
references.locator: Chapter 5, Farkas and duality sections; finite-dimensional alternatives are separated from the local nonlinear argument.

items.title: Convex KKT conditions certify a global minimum and an outward normal
items.statement:
Let $m\ge0$ be an integer. Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and convex,
and suppose the objective $f:U\to\mathbb R$ and inequalities
$g_i:U\to\mathbb R$ $(1\le i\le m)$ are differentiable and convex.
Let the equalities be $Ax=b$ and define the feasible set
$C=\{x\in U:Ax=b,\ g_i(x)\le0\ (1\le i\le m)\}$. If a feasible tuple
$(x_*,\nu,\lambda)$ satisfies the KKT conditions with $\lambda\ge0$, then
$x_*$ is a global minimizer over the feasible set $C$. Moreover,
$-\nabla f(x_*)\in N_C(x_*)$, where the normal cone has the convention of
[[def-kkt-residual-and-normal-cone]].
items.strategy:
1.1 Fix any feasible $y$ and put $d=y-x_*$. Then $Ad=0$. KKT stationarity gives $
abla f(x_*)^Td=-\sum_i\lambda_i
abla g_i(x_*)^Td$. If $\lambda_i=0$ its term is zero. If $\lambda_i>0$, complementarity gives $g_i(x_*)=0$, and [F1] applied to $g_i$ gives $
abla g_i(x_*)^Td\le g_i(y)\le0$. Hence $
abla f(x_*)^Td\ge0$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Applying [F1] to $f$ yields $f(y)\ge f(x_*)+
abla f(x_*)^Td\ge f(x_*)$. Since $y$ was arbitrary, $x_*$ is globally minimizing. Step 1.1 also gives $\langle-
abla f(x_*),y-x_*angle\le0$ for every feasible $y$, which is exactly $-
abla f(x_*)\in N_C(x_*)$ by [F2]. [step 1.1, F1, F2, algebra] ∎

references.title: Boyd and Vandenberghe, Convex Optimization
references.locator: Chapter 5, Sections 5.1–5.2, printed pp. 215–227, weak duality and KKT certificates; Chapter 3, Section 3.1.3, convex gradient inequality.

references.title: Nocedal and Wright, Numerical Optimization, second edition
references.locator: Chapter 12, Section 12.4, printed pp. 348–350, convex programs and global optimality.

items.title: The scaled KKT residual vanishes exactly at KKT tuples
items.statement:
For the program of
[[def-inequality-constrained-program-and-kkt-geometry]] and the residual
of [[def-kkt-residual-and-normal-cone]],
$r_{\mathrm{KKT}}(x,\nu,\lambda)=0$ if and only if
$(x,\nu,\lambda)$ satisfies every KKT condition.
items.strategy:
1.1 If the residual is zero, each summand in [F1] is nonnegative and their sum is zero, so each norm is zero. The stationarity and equality terms then give stationarity and $h(x)=0$. The positive-part term is zero exactly when $g_i(x)\le0$ for every $i$, and the negative-multiplier term is zero exactly when $\lambda_i\ge0$ for every $i$. The last term gives $\lambda_i g_i(x)=0$ coordinatewise. These are all conditions in [F2]. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Conversely, if the KKT conditions hold, every vector inside each norm in [F1] is zero: feasibility makes $h=0$ and $[g]^+=0$, dual feasibility makes $[-\lambda]^+=0$, complementarity makes $\lambda\circ g=0$, and stationarity makes the first vector zero. Thus the residual is zero. [given, F1, F2, algebra] ∎

references.title: Nocedal and Wright, Numerical Optimization, second edition
references.locator: Chapter 12, Section 12.2, printed pp. 327–331; stationarity, primal and dual feasibility, and complementarity.

references.title: Boyd and Vandenberghe, Convex Optimization
references.locator: Chapter 5, Sections 5.1–5.2, KKT and complementarity conventions.

items.title: Strict second-order positivity on the critical cone gives a strict local minimum
items.statement:
For the $C^2$ program of
[[def-inequality-constrained-program-and-kkt-geometry]], suppose $x_*$ is
feasible and has KKT multipliers $(\nu,\lambda)$. If
$$
d^T\nabla_{xx}^2L(x_*,\nu,\lambda)d>0\quad\text{for every nonzero }d\in\mathcal K(x_*,\nu,\lambda),
$$
then $x_*$ is a strict local minimizer. The condition is vacuous when the
critical cone is $\{0\}$; no constraint qualification is assumed.
items.strategy:
1.1 Write $Q(d)=d^T
abla_{xx}^2L(x_*,
u,\lambda)d$ and $S=\{d:\|d\|_2=1\}$. The critical cone intersected with $S$ is closed in $S$ by its linear equalities and inequalities. If this intersection is nonempty, it is compact by [F2], and [F2] gives a minimum $\gamma=\min Q(d)>0$ there. The relatively open set $N=\{u\in S:Q(u)>\gamma/2\}$ contains that intersection. If the intersection is empty, put $N=\varnothing$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 For $k\ge1$, let $D_k$ be the set of unit directions $u=(x-x_*)/\|x-x_*\|_2$ for feasible $x
e x_*$ with $\|x-x_*\|_2<1/k$ and $f(x)\le f(x_*)$. If $D_k$ is empty for some $k$, there is no such point in that neighborhood and strict local minimality holds. Otherwise, if bad points occur arbitrarily close with directions outside $N$, the nonempty nested closed sets $\overline{D_k\setminus N}$ have the finite-intersection property in the compact sphere $S$. By [F3] choose $d\in igcap_k\overline{D_k\setminus N}$; since $N$ is relatively open, $d
otin N$ and $\|d\|_2=1$. [F2, F3, construct]

2.1 For each $k$, the closure property in step 1.2 supplies a direction $u$ with $\|u-d\|_2<1/k$ from a feasible bad point $x=x_*+tu$, where $0<t<1/k$ and $f(x)\le f(x_*)$. Taylor expansion [F4] and equality feasibility imply $Dh(x_*)u=O(t)$; active inequality feasibility gives $Dg_i(x_*)u\le O(t)$ for every active $i$. The objective inequality gives $
abla f(x_*)^Tu\le O(t)$. Letting $k$ grow in these bounds, using $\|u-d\|_2<1/k$ and $t<1/k$, shows $Dh(x_*)d=0$, $Dg_i(x_*)d\le0$ on the active set, and $
abla f(x_*)^Td\le0$. KKT stationarity and [F1] also give $
abla f(x_*)^Td\ge0$, so $d$ is a unit critical direction. This contradicts $d
otin N$: if the critical unit set is empty there is no such $d$, and otherwise every such $d$ belongs to $N$. Hence for some $k_0$, every feasible bad point with $0<\|x-x_*\|_2<1/k_0$ has direction in $N$. [F1, F3, F4, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 If the critical unit set is empty, step 2.1 already excludes all bad points sufficiently near $x_*$, proving strict local minimality. Otherwise, let $\gamma>0$ be as in step 1.1. At a feasible $x=x_*+tu$, KKT gives $L(x_*,
u,\lambda)=f(x_*)$, $
abla_xL(x_*,
u,\lambda)=0$, and $L(x,
u,\lambda)\le f(x)$. For bad points sufficiently close, step 2.1 gives $u\in N$, so $Q(u)>\gamma/2$. The Taylor expansion [F4] of the $C^2$ Lagrangian has a remainder $o(t^2)$, uniformly as $x	o x_*$; after shrinking the neighborhood it yields $L(x,
u,\lambda)>f(x_*)$. This contradicts $L(x,
u,\lambda)\le f(x)\le f(x_*)$. Therefore no distinct feasible point sufficiently near $x_*$ has objective at most $f(x_*)$, proving that $x_*$ is a strict local minimizer. [F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

references.title: Nocedal and Wright, Numerical Optimization, second edition
references.locator: Chapter 12, Section 12.4, Theorem 12.6 and its full proof, printed pp. 345–346; strict positivity on the critical cone needs no constraint qualification.

references.title: Boyd and Vandenberghe, Convex Optimization
references.locator: Chapter 3, Section 3.1.3, the second-order Taylor and convexity tools used in local optimality arguments.

items.title: Slater gives zero duality gap and an attained dual certificate
items.statement:
Consider the finite-dimensional convex program of
[[def-convex-program-duality-and-slater-condition]]. Assume its equality
matrix has independent rows, Slater's condition holds, and the finite primal
value $p^*\in\mathbb R$ is attained at $x_*$. Then there are
$\lambda_*\ge0$ and $\nu_*$ such that
$$q(\lambda_*,\nu_*)=d^*=p^*.$$
Moreover, every inequality multiplier satisfies
$\lambda_{*,i}g_i(x_*)=0$. The Slater and attainment hypotheses do not assert
that a primal minimizer is unique.
items.strategy:
1.1 For perturbations $u\in\mathbb R^m$ and $v\in\mathbb R^p$, define $ P(u,v)=\inf\{f_0(x):x\in D,\ g_i(x)\le u_i\ (1\le i\le m),\ Ax-b=v\}. $ This value function is convex. Indeed, for two perturbations with finite values, choose feasible points with objective within $\epsilon$ of their respective infima. A convex combination of those points lies in $D$, its inequalities and equality residual are bounded by the same convex combination of perturbations, and convexity of $f_0$ bounds its objective. Letting $\epsilon\downarrow0$ proves the convex inequality. If one perturbation value is $-\infty$, arbitrarily low feasible objective values and the same convex-combination argument give value $-\infty$ at each strict convex combination with another feasible perturbation. [given, F1, construct]

1.2 Let $S=\operatorname{aff}D$ and $Y=A(S)-b$. Since the Slater point $x_s$ lies in every relative-interior domain, $x_s$ has a relative neighborhood in $S$ contained in $D$. Each $g_i$ is finite and convex on its domain and continuous near $x_s$ in its affine hull by [F4]; after intersecting finitely many neighborhoods, there are a relative neighborhood $U_s\subseteq D$ of $x_s$ and $\eta>0$ with $g_i(y)<-\eta$ on $U_s$ for every $i$ (take any $\eta>0$ if $m=0$). The affine map $y\mapsto Ay-b$ from $S$ onto $Y$ has a linear right inverse on its direction space: choose preimages of a finite basis of $Y$. Consequently, its image of $U_s$ contains a relative neighborhood $W$ of $0$ in $Y$. For every $v\in W$, choose the corresponding $y\in U_s$; for every $u\in\prod_i(-\eta,\infty)$, that $y$ satisfies $g_i(y)<u_i$ and $Ay-b=v$. Thus $P(u,v)<+\infty$ on a relative neighborhood of $0$ in $Z=\mathbb R^m\times Y$. [given, F1, F4, construct]

2.1 The value $P(0,0)=p^*$ is finite. The convexity from step 1.1 and the neighborhood from step 1.2 imply that $P$ never equals $-\infty$: if $P(z)=-\infty$ for some perturbation $z$, choose a small $\theta>0$ so $-\theta z/(1-\theta)$ lies in that neighborhood. Convexity would give $P(0)\le\theta P(z)+(1-\theta)P(-\theta z/(1-\theta))=-\infty$, contrary to finiteness. Hence $P$ is proper and $0\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}P)$ relative to $Z$. By [F3] there is a linear functional $\ell(u,v)=a^Tu+c(v)$ on $Z$ such that $P(u,v)\ge p^*+a^Tu+c(v)$. [F1, F3, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Relaxing one inequality right-hand side cannot increase the infimum, so $P(te_i,0)\le P(0,0)=p^*$ for small $t>0$. The support inequality in step 2.1 gives $P(te_i,0)\ge p^*+t a_i$, hence $a_i\le0$. Define $\lambda_*=-a\ge0$ and extend $c$ from the finite-dimensional subspace $Y$ to a linear functional on $\mathbb R^p$ by extending a basis; write the negative of this extension as $\nu_*^T$. For any $x\in D$, the perturbation $(g(x),Ax-b)$ is feasible using $x$ itself, so $ f_0(x)\ge P(g(x),Ax-b)\ge p^*+a^Tg(x)+c(Ax-b). $ Thus $L(x,\lambda_*,\nu_*)\ge p^*$ for all $x$, and $q(\lambda_*,\nu_*)\ge p^*$. [F1, step 2.1, algebra, construct]

4.1 At the primal minimizer, weak duality [F2] and feasibility give $ p^*\le q(\lambda_*,\nu_*)\le L(x_*,\lambda_*,\nu_*)= p^*+\sum_i\lambda_{*,i}g_i(x_*)\le p^*. $ Every inequality is therefore equality. Since every summand $\lambda_{*,i}g_i(x_*)$ is nonpositive, their sum being zero forces each one to be zero. Thus $q(\lambda_*,\nu_*)=p^*=d^*$, the dual supremum is attained, and complementarity holds. [F1, F2, step 3.1, given, algebra] ∎

references.title: Boyd and Vandenberghe, Convex Optimization
references.locator: Chapter 5, Sections 5.2.3 and 5.3.2, printed pp. 226–227 and 235–236; Slater zero gap, dual attainment, and the perturbation-value proof.

references.title: Zhiyuan Li, Convex Optimization, Lecture 5: Lagrange Multipliers and KKT
references.locator: Theorem 5.3 and its full proof, including the relative-interior perturbation domain and computation of the dual objective.

items.title: LICQ implies MFCQ and makes KKT multipliers unique
items.statement:
For the $C^2$ program of
[[def-inequality-constrained-program-and-kkt-geometry]], LICQ at a feasible
point $x$ implies MFCQ there. If $x$ is a local minimizer, its KKT
multipliers exist and are unique.
items.strategy:
1.1 Put the equality-gradient rows and all active inequality-gradient rows into a matrix $M$. By [F1], its rows are independent. If $M$ has no rows, take $w=0$. Otherwise $MM^T$ is invertible: for nonzero $\eta$, $\eta^TMM^T\eta=\|M^T\eta\|_2^2>0$ by row independence. For the target vector $r$ whose equality entries are $0$ and whose active inequality entries are $-1$, set $w=M^T(MM^T)^{-1}r$. Then $Mw=r$, so $Dh(x)w=0$ and $Dg_i(x)w=-1<0$ for every active $i$. This is MFCQ. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 If $x$ is a local minimizer, [F2] now supplies at least one KKT pair $(
u,\lambda)$. [F2, step 1.1, given]

3.1 Suppose $(
u,\lambda)$ and $(\widehat
u,\widehat\lambda)$ are two KKT pairs at $x$. Complementarity and strict negativity of each inactive $g_i(x)$ force both corresponding multipliers to be $0$. Subtracting the two stationarity equations leaves a linear combination of the equality gradients and active inequality gradients equal to $0$. LICQ makes every coefficient zero, hence $
u=\widehat
u$ and $\lambda=\widehat\lambda$. [F1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

references.title: Nocedal and Wright, Numerical Optimization, second edition
references.locator: Chapter 12, Sections 12.2 and 12.5, printed pp. 328–330 and 352–353; LICQ, MFCQ, and uniqueness of multipliers.

references.title: Zhiyuan Li, Convex Optimization, Lecture 5: Lagrange Multipliers and KKT
references.locator: KKT definitions and multiplier discussion; the rank argument below is given locally.

items.title: Second-order necessity on the critical cone under LICQ
items.statement:
For the $C^2$ program of
[[def-inequality-constrained-program-and-kkt-geometry]], let $x_*$ be a
local minimizer satisfying LICQ, and let $(\nu,\lambda)$ be its KKT
multipliers. Then
$$
d^T\nabla_{xx}^2L(x_*,\nu,\lambda)d\ge0\qquad\text{for every }d\in\mathcal K(x_*,\nu,\lambda).
$$
items.strategy:
1.1 If $d=0$ the result is immediate, so assume $d
e0$. Let $P=\{i\in I(x_*):\lambda_i>0\}$ and $Z=\{i\in I(x_*):\lambda_i=0,\ Dg_i(x_*)d=0\}$. Put $H=(h,(g_i)_{i\in P})$. By LICQ the rows of $DH(x_*)$, together with the rows $Dg_i(x_*)$ for $i\in Z$, are independent. Thus the combined finite-dimensional linear map is onto. Choose $z$ solving $ Dh(x_*)z+D^2h(x_*)[d,d]=0,\quad Dg_i(x_*)z+D^2g_i(x_*)[d,d]=0\ (i\in P), $ and $ Dg_i(x_*)z+D^2g_i(x_*)[d,d]=-1\ (i\in Z). $ The first two groups say $DH(x_*)z+D^2H(x_*)[d,d]=0$. [given, F1, F2, construct]

2.1 By [F3] there is a $C^2$ curve $\gamma$ with $H(\gamma(t))=H(x_*)$, $\gamma(0)=x_*$, $\gamma'(0)=d$, and $\gamma''(0)=z$. For $i\in P$ the corresponding active inequality is exactly fixed at zero. An active $i
otin P$ has $\lambda_i=0$; by [F2], either $Dg_i(x_*)d<0$, giving $g_i(\gamma(t))=tDg_i(x_*)d+O(t^2)<0$, or $i\in Z$, giving $g_i(\gamma(t))=-t^2/2+o(t^2)<0$. Inactive inequalities remain strict by continuity. Hence $\gamma(t)$ is feasible for all sufficiently small $t>0$. [step 1.1, F2, F3, F4, algebra]

2.2 Taylor expansion [F4], criticality $
abla f(x_*)^Td=0$, and $\gamma(t)=x_*+td+	frac12t^2z+o(t^2)$ give $ f(\gamma(t))-f(x_*)= 	frac12t^2 igl(
abla f(x_*)^Tz+ d^T
abla^2 f(x_*)d igr)+o(t^2). $ Stationarity gives $
abla f(x_*)^Tz=-
u^TDh(x_*)z-\sum_{i\in P}\lambda_iDg_i(x_*)z$. The jet equations in step 1.1 therefore make the coefficient in parentheses equal to $d^T
abla_{xx}^2L(x_*,
u,\lambda)d$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, F4, algebra]

3.1 Local minimality gives $f(\gamma(t))-f(x_*)\ge0$ for small $t>0$. If the displayed Lagrangian quadratic form were negative, step 2.2 would make this difference negative for all sufficiently small positive $t$, a contradiction. Thus the quadratic form is nonnegative, as claimed. [step 2.1, step 2.2, given, assume-contra, discharge-contradiction] ∎

references.title: Nocedal and Wright, Numerical Optimization, second edition
references.locator: Chapter 12, Section 12.4, Theorem 12.5 and its full proof, printed pp. 343–344; LICQ and critical-cone second-order necessity.

references.title: J. M. Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds
references.locator: Regular-level local graph theorem, used to realize equality-feasible curves with a prescribed second-order jet.

title: Inequality kkt duality and optimality certificates — Examples

items.title: A true minimizer with no KKT multipliers when MFCQ fails
items.statement:
Minimize $f(x,y)=x$ subject to
$g(x,y)=y^2-x^3\le0$. The origin is a global minimizer, but it has no KKT
multiplier because the active constraint gradient vanishes there.
items.strategy:
1.1 If $g(x,y)\le0$, then $y^2\le x^3$. Since $y^2\ge0$, this forces $x^3\ge0$, hence $x\ge0$. The origin is feasible and has objective $0$, so it is a global minimizer. [given, algebra]

1.2 At $(0,0)$ the constraint is active, $
abla f(0,0)=(1,0)$, and $
abla g(0,0)=(-3x^2,2y)|_{(0,0)}=(0,0)$. Thus $
abla f+\lambda
abla g=(1,0)
e0$ for every $\lambda\ge0$; no KKT multiplier exists. MFCQ also fails because $Dg(0,0)w=0$ for every direction $w$, so no direction strictly decreases the active constraint. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 This does not contradict [F2]: the origin is a local and global minimizer, but the MFCQ hypothesis fails, and the direct stationarity calculation proves multiplier existence cannot be inferred here. [step 1.1, step 1.2, F2] ∎

references.title: Nocedal and Wright, Numerical Optimization, second edition
references.locator: Chapter 12, Sections 12.2 and 12.5, printed pp. 328–329 and 351–353; constraint qualifications are required for first-order multiplier existence.

references.title: Boyd and Vandenberghe, Convex Optimization
references.locator: Chapter 5, Sections 5.2–5.3, printed pp. 221–236; constraints qualifications and the separate Slater branch.

items.title: A closed convex program with a positive duality gap when Slater fails
items.statement:
Define the extended-real perspective
$$
\phi(x,y)=\begin{cases}x^2/y,&y>0,\\0,&(x,y)=(0,0),\\+\infty,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}
$$
Minimize $f_0(x,y)=e^{-x}$ subject to $\phi(x,y)\le0$. Both functions are
proper closed convex, the primal minimum is $1$, Slater fails, and the
Lagrangian dual value is $0$.
items.strategy:
1.1 The epigraph of $\phi$ is exactly $E=\{(x,y,t):y\ge0,\ t\ge0,\ x^2\le yt\}$. For $y>0$ this is the inequality $t\ge x^2/y$; when $y=0$ it forces $x=0$ and $t\ge0$; for $y<0$ it is empty. Thus $E$ is closed, being defined by continuous non-strict inequalities. It is convex: if $|x_j|\le\sqrt{y_jt_j}$ for $j=1,2$, then for $0\le\theta\le1$, $ |\theta x_1+(1-\theta)x_2| \le\theta\sqrt{y_1t_1}+(1-\theta)\sqrt{y_2t_2} \le\sqrt{(\theta y_1+(1-\theta)y_2) (\theta t_1+(1-\theta)t_2)} $ by Cauchy–Schwarz. Therefore $\phi$ is closed convex. The objective is continuous and has second derivative $e^{-x}>0$ in $x$, so it is closed convex and proper as well. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 On its domain $\phi\ge0$. If $y>0$, $\phi(x,y)\le0$ forces $x=0$; if $y=0$, finiteness already forces $x=0$. Hence the feasible set is $\{(0,y):y\ge0\}$ and $f_0=1$ throughout it, so $p^*=1$ and the primal minimum is attained, for example at $(0,0)$. No point has $\phi(x,y)<0$, so Slater fails. [given, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For $\lambda\ge0$, every point in the Lagrangian domain has $e^{-x}+\lambda\phi(x,y)\ge0$, so $q(\lambda)\ge0$. At $\lambda=0$, taking $x\to+\infty$ gives $q(0)=0$. For $\lambda>0$, take $(x_k,y_k)=(k,k^3)$; then $e^{-x_k}+\lambda\phi(x_k,y_k)=e^{-k}+\lambda/k\to0$, so again $q(\lambda)=0$. Therefore $d^*=\sup_{\lambda\ge0}q(\lambda)=0$ and the positive duality gap is $p^*-d^*=1$. This does not contradict [F2], because its Slater hypothesis fails. [F1, F2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The calculation gives a closed convex primal problem with attained finite optimum and a strict gap; the missing strict-feasibility condition is exactly the boundary that blocks the Slater theorem's certificate. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

references.title: Zhiyuan Li, Convex Optimization, Lecture 5: Lagrange Multipliers and KKT
references.locator: Example 5.5, lines 418–446; the source's open-domain perspective constraint has primal value 1 and dual value 0. This carrier adds its closed perspective boundary and verifies it independently.

references.title: Boyd and Vandenberghe, Convex Optimization
references.locator: Chapter 5, Sections 5.2.3 and 5.3.2, printed pp. 226–236; Slater assumptions and strong-duality conclusion.

items.title: Active-set quadratic with an exact KKT certificate
items.statement:
Minimize
$$f(x_1,x_2)=\tfrac12\bigl((x_1+1)^2+(x_2-2)^2\bigr)$$
subject to $g(x_1,x_2)=-x_1\le0$. The point $x_*=(0,2)$ has one active
constraint and multiplier $\lambda_*=1$.
items.strategy:
1.1 The constraint is feasible exactly when $x_1\ge0$. At $x_*=(0,2)$ it is active, and $\nabla f(x_*)=(1,0)$ while $\nabla g(x_*)=(-1,0)$. Therefore $\nabla f(x_*)+\lambda_*\nabla g(x_*)=0$ for $\lambda_*=1\ge0$, and $\lambda_*g(x_*)=0$. The active gradient is nonzero, so the one-row LICQ holds. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 The quadratic is convex and differentiable. Primal feasibility and the multiplier checks in step 1.1 satisfy the hypotheses of [F2], so $x_*$ is a global minimizer. Directly, for every feasible $x$, $ f(x)-f(x_*)=x_1+\tfrac12x_1^2+\tfrac12(x_2-2)^2\ge0, $ with equality only when $x_1=0$ and $x_2=2$. Thus the minimizer is unique, and [F1] makes $\lambda_*=1$ the unique multiplier. [step 1.1, F1, F2, algebra]

3.1 The active-set KKT certificate is exact: it proves the unique global minimizer $x_*=(0,2)$ and its unique nonnegative multiplier $\lambda_*=1$. [step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

references.title: Nocedal and Wright, Numerical Optimization, second edition
references.locator: Chapter 12, Sections 12.1–12.2, printed pp. 317–331; active inequalities and first-order KKT certificates.

references.title: Boyd and Vandenberghe, Convex Optimization
references.locator: Chapter 5, Sections 5.1 and 5.5, KKT and global convex optimality certificates.

items.title: An unconstrained KKT point that is a saddle
items.statement:
With no constraints, let $f(x_1,x_2)=x_1^2-x_2^2$. The origin satisfies
the KKT stationarity equation, but is a saddle point rather than a local
minimum.
items.strategy:
1.1 The gradient is $\nabla f(x_1,x_2)=(2x_1,-2x_2)$, so $\nabla f(0,0)=0$ and the origin is KKT. With no constraints, $\mathcal L_C(0)=\mathbb R^2$ and $\mathcal K(0)=\mathbb R^2$. The Hessian is $\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&-2\end{pmatrix}$, whose quadratic form at $d=(0,1)$ is $-2$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 For every $t\ne0$, $f(t,0)=t^2>0=f(0,0)$, while $f(0,t)=-t^2<0=f(0,0)$. Both points approach the origin as $t\to0$, so the origin is neither a local minimum nor a local maximum. The negative critical curvature also violates the necessary condition in [F2], and strict positivity required by its sufficient condition fails. [given, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Thus stationarity alone is not an optimality certificate: this KKT point is a saddle. [step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎
